answers.text:
Transfer entropy is a specific information-theoretic measure — introduced by Schreiber, cited here as reference [11] — that captures directed information flow between two variables over time. As the passage right after this selection explains, it measures how much the past activity of one neuron accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron, conditioned on that second neuron's own past, and is read as the transfer entropy from the source's past to the target's future.

The key word is "directed." Unlike mutual information, which just measures whether two neurons' activity patterns are statistically related without saying which one is influencing which, transfer entropy asks a time-ordered question: does knowing what neuron X did a moment ago help predict what neuron Y will do next, above and beyond what Y's own recent history already tells you? The article makes this contrast explicit a few sentences earlier, noting that mutual information does not, however, quantify information transfer between the neurons, as it is an undirected measure that describes the instantaneous dependency between two variables and has no notion of the time-directed structure that we intuitively understand as "transfer" or "flow." Transfer entropy is built specifically to fill that gap, which is why the article distinguishes them as two complementary tools: mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity.

In the larger argument of the paper, transfer entropy plays a specific supporting role: it is used to trace which neurons send information to which others, so that later the authors can identify triads — two source neurons feeding into one target — for the partial information decomposition (PID) analysis that is the real subject of the review. So transfer entropy is not itself the method the paper is introducing; it is the tool used beforehand to reconstruct the wiring of information flow that PID then dissects into redundant, unique, and synergistic components.

answers.asked: Information-theoretic tools such as mutual information [10] and transfer entropy [11] are well suited to this purpose.
answers.text:
This is introducing the two basic tools the article uses to track how information moves between neurons, before it gets to the more advanced machinery (partial information decomposition) that the rest of the paper is really about.

Mutual information and transfer entropy answer different questions. As the article explains a moment later, mutual information "can be thought of as a nonlinear correlation between two patterns of activity" — it tells you how much knowing one neuron's activity reduces your uncertainty about another's, but it's symmetric and has no sense of time or direction, so it can't say who is influencing whom. Transfer entropy fixes that: it measures "how much the past activity of one neuron... accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron", conditioned on that second neuron's own past, so it captures directional flow rather than mere co-variation. The article later sharpens this distinction by noting that "mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity" — the first says two neurons' activity is statistically linked, the second says information is actually propagating from one to the other over time.

The two numbered citations point to the original technical sources for each measure: mutual information traces back to classical information theory, and transfer entropy to a specific paper that formalized it as a directional measure. Placing them side by side here sets up the section's larger point: these tools let you track information moving through a circuit, but as the next section argues, tracking flow is not the same as understanding how neurons actually process or combine that information — which is the gap partial information decomposition is introduced to fill.

answers.asked: What does "transfer entropy" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this piece, transfer entropy is a directional measure of information flow between two neurons: it tells you how much the past activity of one neuron reduces uncertainty about another neuron's immediate future, over and above what that second neuron's own past already told you. The formal definition is given as transfer entropy is well suited to measuring how much the past activity of one neuron accounts for the immediate future activity of another neuron, conditioned on Y's own past, and is read as the transfer entropy from X's past to Y's future. The article stresses that TE is understood as quantifying how much the past of the source variable reduces our uncertainty about the future of the target variable, after accounting for information disclosed by the target variable's own past (autocorrelation).

The article draws a sharp contrast with mutual information here: mutual information just measures instantaneous statistical dependence between two neurons with no sense of direction or time, so it functions as a measure of "functional connectivity," whereas mutual information does not quantify information transfer between the neurons, as it is an undirected measure that describes the instantaneous dependency between two variables and has no notion of the time-directed structure that we intuitively understand as "transfer" or "flow." Transfer entropy fills that gap: whereas mutual information is a measure of functional connectivity, transfer entropy measures effective connectivity — in other words, transfer entropy provides a measure of information propagation.

Why it matters to the larger argument: transfer entropy is the tool the authors use to turn a raw spike recording into a directed "effective network" of who-influences-whom, which is the necessary first step before any of the partial information decomposition (PID) analysis can happen. In the empirical work, the authors rendered the single-unit-level functional recording into an effective network, capturing the microcircuit dynamics using transfer entropy, and from that identified all triads consisting of two source neurons connecting to a common target neuron, which is exactly where PID is then applied. Later, transfer entropy itself becomes a variable in the analysis: the authors ask whether the amount of synergy in a triad tracks the amount of feedforward transfer entropy, finding that synergy was strongly correlated with the amount of information propagation, and the amount of synergy observed in a given triad was reliably about a quarter of the transfer entropy for that triad. So transfer entropy plays a double role in the argument: it is the method for building the networks the whole study is conducted on, and it is one of the key covariates the paper uses to show that information *processing* (synergy) is tied to information *flow* (transfer entropy) rather than being independent of it.

The article also flags a limitation tied to this measure: the effective networks used in the in vitro studies were built with pairwise (bivariate) transfer entropy, and it has been shown that bivariate analyses overestimate the significance of bivariate edges, which the authors list as a caveat on the empirical results built on top of it.

Synergistic here describes one of the three ways information can be shared among neurons in this framework, and it's the mode the paper cares about most. The abstract says "PID reveals redundant, unique, and synergistic modes by which neurons integrate information from multiple sources." Synergy is singled out because it "quantifies the 'higher-order' information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source."

Later in the article this gets made precise: if you look at two input neurons feeding a target, you can measure how much each one alone tells you about the target's future state, and also how much the two together tell you. Synergy is the surplus — the part of that joint information that only shows up when you look at the two inputs' *combined pattern*, not when you look at them one at a time. The article's own example is a target neuron that fires only when its two inputs are in a particular joint configuration; neither input's individual state predicts that outcome, but the pair does. That surplus is what's meant by synergistic information, and the authors treat it as evidence that the neuron is doing something like a genuine "computation" on its inputs, rather than just adding them up — this is the contrast the summary draws when it notes "neurons do not appear to blindly sum the number of inputs and fire in response to the total... but instead they are also sensitive to the particular patterns of incoming stimuli."

The word will keep recurring through the rest of the piece (rich clubs, recurrent connections, timescale effects, etc.) as the article's main lens for asking where and how neural circuits actually process, rather than just relay, information.

answers.asked: PID reveals redundant, unique, and synergistic modes by which neurons integrate information from multiple sources.
answers.text:
This sentence names the three "modes" that partial information decomposition (PID) sorts information into, and it's worth pausing on what each means, since the rest of the article builds directly on this split.

When a target neuron receives signals from two or more source neurons, the total information those sources carry about the target's future activity can be broken into non-overlapping pieces. As the article puts it, Red(X₁, X₂;Y) is the information about Y that could be learned by observing X₁ or X₂, Unq(Xᵢ;Y) is the information about Y that could only be learned by observing Xᵢ, and Syn(X₁, X₂;Y) is the information about Y that can only be learned by observing the joint states of X₁ and X₂ together. So redundant information is duplicated across sources (either one alone would tell you the same thing), unique information is what only one particular source can tell you, and synergistic information is a kind of bonus that only shows up when you look at the sources' patterns together, not from either one separately.

The synergistic mode is the one the authors care most about, because it's the signature of genuine computation rather than mere pass-through of a signal: We focus particularly on the synergistic mode, which quantifies the "higher-order" information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source. The intuition, developed later in the piece, is that if the whole (the joint information from all sources together) is bigger than the sum of what each source provides individually, that surplus is synergy, and it means the target neuron is doing something like integrating or combining its inputs into a new pattern, rather than just summing them.

This three-way split is the core move of the whole review: everything from the rich-club findings to the primate behavioral results later in the article is really asking "under what circuit conditions does synergy (as opposed to redundancy or uniqueness) go up or down?"

answers.asked: What does "synergistic" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
"Synergistic" (or synergy) refers to information about a target neuron's future that only shows up when you look at the joint, combined pattern of its input neurons together — it is invisible if you examine each input neuron's information on its own. The glossary for this piece defines it this way: synergy is treated as information "that only appears when they are considered together," and is distinguished from redundant information (which any one source could supply alone) and unique information (which only one particular source supplies).

The article builds this idea directly from the mutual information math: the joint information that a set of parent neurons carries about a target is not necessarily equal to the sum of what each parent carries individually. As the piece puts it, "it cannot be assumed that the joint mutual information (the 'whole') is reducible to a sum of all its component marginal 'parts'." When the whole exceeds the sum of the parts, "there is some information about Y that is disclosed by the joint state of all the neurons that is not disclosed by any individual parent. In this case, the system exhibits synergistic dynamics, and the target neuron can be thought of as performing a kind of integrating 'computation' on all of its inputs considered jointly."

That last move — equating synergy with "computation" — is why the concept matters to the whole argument. Ordinary information-flow measures like transfer entropy can track how much information passes from source to target, but the article argues they are "limited in its ability to reveal how different streams of information 'interact' and how neurons produce novel or modified information from multiple sources." Synergy is offered as the missing piece: a way to quantify information processing itself, rather than mere transmission, and the paper explicitly says it focuses on the synergistic mode as "the mode which quantifies the 'higher-order' information carried in the patterns of multiple inputs and is not reducible to input from any single source."

The empirical sections then use synergy as their main dependent variable: they show it is elevated in densely connected "rich club" neurons, increases with recurrent connectivity, and rises then falls as the correlation between converging inputs grows "Unambiguously, rich club triads processed more information than triads outside rich clubs. Numerically, the triads inside the rich clubs had 2.7 times the amount of synergy as the triads not in the rich club". In the summary, the authors make the stakes explicit: the presence of synergy shows that "neurons do not appear to blindly sum the number of inputs and fire in response to the total (as would be expected from a basic threshold model or complex contagion model), but instead they are also sensitive to the particular patterns of incoming stimuli." So synergy is not just a technical byproduct of the decomposition — it's the quantity the whole review uses to argue that neurons genuinely "compute" on their inputs rather than just relaying them.
